title: 《高等微積分》第 63 集｜壓縮映射不動點定理｜Loomis & Sternberg 第 4 章 §9
description:
本集是 Loomis 與 Sternberg《Advanced Calculus》第 4 章第 9 節「壓縮映射不動點定理」的前半（書頁 228 到 230，定理 9.1、推論 1 到 4、定理 9.2、定理 9.3）。第 9 節的內容收在書頁 234，234 到 236 是習題 9.1 到 9.13。

書上說這條定理很簡單、很漂亮，而它要做三件事：補完隱函數定理的證明、第 6 章拿來證常微分方程的存在唯一性，還有跟 Newton 法比較。定義是：K 是度量空間到自己的 Lipschitz 映射，而且常數嚴格小於一。

壓縮至多只有一個不動點，證明只有兩行：兩個不動點的距離等於它們的像的距離，不超過 C 倍，移項就得到一減 C 乘那個距離小於等於零。值得注意的是，這一段完全沒有用到完備性——唯一性是壓縮這個條件自己給的。

定理 9.1：非空的完備度量空間上，壓縮有唯一的不動點。存在性是造出來的：隨便取一個起點，反覆作用 K。相鄰兩項的距離每走一步就縮小 C 倍，所以第 n 對的距離不超過 C 的 n 次方乘 δ；把中間那些距離用幾何級數加起來，就得到 Cauchy 的估計。完備性是在這裡才需要的。

接下來四條推論把定理搬到實際會遇到的情況。實際的映射常常只在某一點附近是壓縮，所以要先確認那個鄰域被送進自己：推論 1 說，閉球上的壓縮只要把球心移動的距離不超過一減 C 乘半徑，不動點就落在球裡；證明就是 C 乘 r 加上一減 C 乘 r 剛好等於 r 這一個加法。推論 2 是開球的版本。推論 3 給距離的估計：K 把 x 移動了 d，那麼 x 到不動點的距離不超過 d 除以一減 C。推論 4 讓壓縮帶一個參數，結論是不動點連續地依賴參數；證明就是把推論 3 接上去。推論 2 與推論 4 合起來就是定理 9.2，那才是後面真正拿來用的形式。

最後補完隱函數定理。定理 9.3：G 在某一點等於零，而且它在那裡的第二個偏微分可逆。令 K 是 η 減去那個偏微分的反元素乘上 G，K 的不動點正好就是 G 等於零的解。關鍵在於 K 對第二個變數的微分在那一點正好是零——那就是把一階項消掉的意思；因為它連續，附近就有一個球讓它的範數不超過二分之一，均值定理再把 K 變成壓縮。

title: Advanced Calculus, Episode 63 | The Contraction Mapping Fixed-Point Theorem | Ch. 4, §9
description:
This episode is the first part of section 9 of chapter 4, the contraction mapping fixed-point theorem, pages 228 to 230 of Loomis and Sternberg's Advanced Calculus, covering Theorem 9.1, Corollaries 1 through 4, Theorem 9.2 and Theorem 9.3. Section 9's content ends on page 234; pages 234 to 236 are exercises 9.1 to 9.13.

The book calls the theorem very simple and elegant, and it has three jobs: to complete the proof of the implicit-function theorem, to give existence and uniqueness for differential equations in chapter 6, and to be set beside Newton's method. The definition: K is a Lipschitz mapping of a metric space into itself whose constant is strictly under one.

A contraction has at most one fixed point, in two lines: two fixed points are as far apart as their images, which is at most C times as far, and rearranging gives one minus C times that distance being at most zero. Worth noticing is that completeness appears nowhere in this argument. Uniqueness comes from the contraction condition alone.

Theorem 9.1: on a nonempty complete metric space a contraction has a unique fixed point. Existence is constructed: pick any starting point and apply K over and over. Each step shrinks the gap between consecutive terms by a factor of C, so the n-th gap is at most C to the n times delta, and summing the gaps between with a geometric series gives the Cauchy estimate. Completeness is what is needed here.

Four corollaries then carry the theorem to the situations actually met. A map is often a contraction only near some point, so the neighbourhood has to be checked to go into itself. Corollary 1: on a closed ball, a contraction that moves the center at most one minus C times the radius has its fixed point inside that ball, and the proof is the single addition C times r plus one minus C times r equals r. Corollary 2 is the open version. Corollary 3 estimates a distance: if K moves x a distance d, then x is within d over one minus C of the fixed point. Corollary 4 gives the contraction a parameter and concludes that the fixed point depends continuously on it, by hooking Corollary 3 on. Corollaries 2 and 4 combine into Theorem 9.2, the form actually used later.

Finally the implicit-function theorem is finished. Theorem 9.3: G vanishes at a point where its second partial differential is invertible. Let K be eta minus the inverse of that differential applied to G; the fixed points of K are exactly the solutions of G equals zero. The key is that the differential of K in its second variable vanishes at that point, which is what killing the first-order term means. Being continuous, it stays under one half on a nearby ball, and the mean value theorem then makes K a contraction.
